title: Project Environments: centralize workflows
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Build project environments
Skill:

Construct environment build file
Centralize conda envs

Why:

The ability to manage conda envs and global variables across projects

title: Project Environments: centralize workflows
text:
Need for project environments


MRI software often requires:

Global variables

FreeSurfer: SUBJECTS_DIR, FREESURFER_HOME, FS_LICENSE
FSL: FSLDIR
fMRIPrep: TEMPLATEFLOW_HOME

Binary access in PATH

AFNI, FSL, c3d, ANTs


Conflicts arise between on-going and new projects

OK solution: change .bashrc when switching projects
Better solution: build project environment from script

Utility: project environment build script can be shared and versioned

title: Project Environments: centralize workflows
text:
Contents of project environments



Load modules
Software versions
Software configuration
PATH updates
Conda activation
Project globals
User messages



#!/bin/bash

# Load, configure FreeSurfer
module load freesurfer/8.0
export SUBJECTS_DIR=/users/$(whoami)/projects
export FS_LICENSE=/users/$(whoami)/research_bin/license.txt
mkdir -p $SUBJECTS_DIR
source $FREESURFER_HOME/SetUpFreeSurfer.sh

# Update path
PATH=${PATH}:\
/users/$(whoami)/research_bin

export PATH

# User globals
SQL_PASS=$(cat ~/.ssh/pass_sql)
RSA_WS=~/.ssh/id_rsa_ws

# Load project conda env
conda activate proj_env


Following this example will require a FreeSurfer License stored at the appropriate location.

title: Project Environments: centralize workflows
text:
Access environments



Activate via source

Proj environment configuration is available to all subshells
E.g. scheduled jobs - no longer need to manage module across multiple job files!

Personal preference: set an alias to activate environments

title: Project Environments: centralize workflows
text:
Save and share



Save environment script somewhere useful

Preferably in ‘env’ directory of code base
Versioning helps reproducibility and replicability

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn to schedule flexible jobs
Skill:

Pass and capture arguments
Redirect output and error messages
Build wrapper and job scripts
Submit and check jobs

Why:

Deploy a common workflow for all subjects
Protect important scripts from requiring edits

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Capture positional arguments



Recall anatomy of shell command:

$ CMD OPT PARAM
$ mkdir -p foo/bar

Commands have 0-indexed positions

0: mkdir
1: -p
2: foo/bar

Positional arguments can be accessed in scripts

Held in special variable $[index]
e.g. $0, $1, $2 …

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Use positional arguments



Assign positional argument to variable
Use variable in script workflow

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Redirect output: STDOUT



STDOUT: output of succesful jobs (exit status 0)
Designated via &1
Normally &1 is the terminal window
Can be redirected to a file with >

>: overwrites
>>: appends

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Redirect output: STDERR



STDERR: output of failed jobs (exit status >0)
Designated via 2>
Normally 2> is the terminal window
Can be redirected to a file with 2>

2> err.log: send STDERR to err.log
2>&1: send STDERR to same location as STDOUT
cmd > out.log 2>&1: Send STDOUT and STDERR to out.log






Notice:

Line 7 printed to err.log
Line 8 printed to terminal

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Job Scripts



Compute environments involve scheduled jobs

e.g. execute workflow A for subjects 1, 2, and 3

OK: edit job scripts for each subject
Better: pass subject number to job script
Job script purpose:

Request resources
Receive arguments
Execute workflow

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Modules



CRC supplies software packages as modules

module avail: See available modules
module load foo: Load module ‘foo’

Common: Load modules in job script

After resource request

Preferred: Load in project environment

(Lecture 11 [TBD])

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Wrapper Scripts



Wrapper script purpose:

Submits job script by envoking qsub command
Passes arguments to the job script

Used as the researcher-editable file

No need to edit job script

Research could pass args to wrapper script

(more advanced)

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Make log directory



Scheduled job runs on non-interactive node

STDOUT and STDERR are sent to [job_name].o[job_id]

Redirect STDOUT and STDERR with -o and -e options

CRC qsub configuration directs 2>&1

Good habit to organize STDOUT/ERR in logging directory

Named for job
Time stamp helps trouble shoot
See here for information on date

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Check status: qstat



Check status of submitted jobs with qstat

qstat -u username: status for all user jobs
qstat -j jobid: status for specific jobs

Number of statuses possible:

r: job is running
qw: job is queued, waiting for resources
Eqw: invalid job

See more options here




Set an alias for things your type often!

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Delete jobs: qdel



Sometimes necessary to kill jobs

Incorrect specification
Syntax error (e.g. no increment in while loops)

Determine job ID with qstat
qdel jobid: Terminates specified job
See more options here

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Long queue times



Sometimes jobs queue (status qw) for a long time

Beginning of semster (students learning)
End of semester (students running final projects)
Teams conducting large analyses
Your request is large

Tips:

Optimize resource usage
Consider parent and child jobs
Consider job arrays
Lower cluster use at night, on weekends

qstat: (without options) check entire queue




See here for using | (pipes)

title: Cluster Computing: pass arguments, schedule and check jobs
text:
Check available resources



free_nodes.sh -G: Check usage of CPUs and nodes
qstat -u user -g t: Check utilized nodes

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn about different shells and how to interact with them
Skill:

Types of shells
Targeting shells
Global variables
Aliases

Why:

Control information in workflows
Prepare for cluster computing
Increase user comfort

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Environment Configuration



Three important build files in $HOME

.profile (OSx)
.bash_profile
.bashrc

Purpose

Establish shell environments
User customization

Differ in relationship to shell types

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Shells: non/login



Login shell: Initiated when user logs into system

e.g. over SSH connection (cluster)
Builds from ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile

Non-login shell: Subsequent shells after login session

e.g. Terminal tabs, subshells
Builds from ~/.bashrc

Determine login shells status with shopt -q login_shell



shopt -q login_shell && echo login \
    || echo non-login

non-login

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Shells: non/interactive



Interactive shell: Allows user to enter commands

Typical shell experience
Builds from ~/.bashrc

Non-interactive shell: Does not receive commands

e.g. Subshells, commands executed through SSH tunnel
Subshells inherit environment
Log-in, non-interactive build from ~/.bash_profile

Determine interactive shells status with $-

Interactive shells contain “i”




echo $-
[[ $- == *i* ]] && echo interact \
    || echo non-interact

hBc
non-interact

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Complexity of config files



.bash_profile: keep simple due to login processes

common to execute .bashrc in current shell
[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && . ~/.bashrc

.bashrc: user customizations

Update PATH
Set functions
Add aliases




cat ~/.bash_profile | wc -l
cat ~/.bashrc | wc -l

       1
      48

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Executing code, revisited



source or . executes in current shell
./ executes in non-login, non-interactive shell

AND copied environment from current shell



#!/bin/bash
shopt -q login_shell && echo login \
    || echo non-login
[[ $- == *i* ]] && echo interact \
    || echo non-interact









Execution in different shells

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Executing code, more options



$(foo) executes command foo in subshell
bash foo.sh or sh foo.sh to execute script in language-specific subshell
Remote execution in login, non-interactive shell
Point: Relevant to remember how these shell environments build

(.bashrc vs .bash_profile)




my_files=$(ls .)
ssh user@server.com "mkdir ~/test"

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Global variables



Variables only exist in definition shell
Global variables: variables for current and subshells
Defined with export and uses SCREAM_SNAKE_CASE

export FOO_BAR=some_value

Useful for building environments


#!/bin/bash
echo $foo
echo $FOO
export BAR=my_bar









FOO available in subshell, BAR not available in parent shell

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Global variables: Building environments



Important paths for workflows

Software
Templates
Singularity
Reference files

Should be added to .bashrc

(e.g. nano ~/.bashrc)

Rebuild shell to reflect changes

New, or ‘. ~/.bashrc’

env: Print all globals



export FSLDIR=/path/to/fsl/install
export TEMPLATEFLOW=/path/to/templateflow
export SING_FREESURFER=/path/to/freesurfer.simg

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Global variables: PATH



PATH: search locations for matching command to executable
New software: update to PATH needed

.bashrc is common location, .bash_profile is OK

Use : to separate locations

Better to append (beware trailing whitespace)
Avoid prepending (despite enthusiastic install tutorials)

Command based on first match in PATH



PATH=${PATH}:\
/path/to/soft/a:\
/path/to/soft/b:\
/path/to/soft/c

export PATH

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Global variables: PS1



Define, customize the command prompt
Controls text and color, useful for tracking machines

\u for user
\W for current working directory
PS1='[\u-machine: \W]$'

See here for some color codes

Open color with \e[color-code-m
Close color with \e[m
PS1='\e[color-codem[\u-machine: \W]$\e[m'

.bashrc is proper location

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Aliases



Avoid repeated typing by setting alias
Anatomy:

alias
alias name
command(s) in single quotes


alias cdd='cd ~/Desktop; ls'

Should be added to .bashrc

Also common to make ~/.bash_aliases
Remember to source file in .bashrc

Avoid:

Using globals for aliases
Replacing existing commands (e.g. cd)

alias: Print all aliases



alias nb='nano ~/.bashrc'
alias sb='. ~/.bashrc'
alias cl='clear; ls'
alias my_proj='cd /to/my/project/dir; ls'

title: Shells: types, editing, and aliases
text:
Style files (OSx)



Ubuntu comes with file colors (check .bashrc)

Differentiate directories, executables, files

Not the case in OSx
Controlled with globals:

CLICOLOR: turn on/off colors
LSCOLORS: set colors for ls output

Specify in .bashrc



export CLICOLOR=1
export LSCOLORS=GxFxCxDxBxegedabagaced

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn to save and execute work
Skill:

Write scripts and manage permissions
Execute in desired shell

Why:

Workflow replicability, transparency
Increase complexity of commands while decreasing researcher effort

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Scripts




Enter commands into terminal:

Fine for few, short commands
Many - tedious, error prone

Scripting:

Save commands into file (script)
Execute file

Utility:

Reusable scripts
Error checking
Decrease typing

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Create New Script




touch: Create new file

Update write-time for existing files

nano: Create and open file with built-in editor

Other built-ins: vi, vim, emacs
Exit sequence:

ctrl-x: save and exit
y: overwrite
specify name, return


Specify interpreter via #!

Provides path to executable

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
CHMOD




CHange MODe of files
ls -l shows file permissions by group

User, group, other

Numeric access (8 bit):

read (4), write (2), execute (1)
rw- = 6
rwxr-xr-x = 755

chmod 755 new_script.sh - detail permission for each group
chmod +x new_script.sh - assign execute to all groups

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Execution




Execute in different shells

current vs sub shell

Relevant for variable availability
Method 1: source or dot execution

source new_script.sh
. new_script.sh is preferred
Executes script in current shell
Variables available for future use
Ideal for creating environments
Overrides permissions (discouraged)

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Execution, cont’d




Method 2: direct execution

./new_script.sh
Executes script in sub-shell
Variables only exist in sub-shell
Ideal for executing independent scripts

Method 3: interpreter execution

bash new_script.sh
Executes script in specified shell
Discouraged, specify interpreter in script

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
IDEs




Integrated Development Environments
Editor: syntax highlighting, formatting, error detection
Compiler or Interpreter: build and execute
Extra features:

Testing
Debugging
Visualization
Remote Development

Popular for Bash

Sublime: simple text editor, “free”
VS Code: IDE, plugins for languages, free for research and learning

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Style guides


Individual programming style - “Spaghetti Code”

Difficult to read, maintain, optimize
xkcd comic

Strongly encourage using style guides

Google Style

Reasons:

Increases professionalism
Ability to collaborate
Access to plugins (autoformatter, linter, documentation)
Program faster
Reduce learning curve

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Purpose


Knowledge:

Learn how to store data for future use
Manipulate return values

Skill:

Strings and variables
Brace expansion
Manipulating variable information

Why:

Useful for building organized directory trees, file names
Commonly desirous to extract information from file name

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Strings




Series of key strokes:

abcd1234
Hello World

Good to avoid spaces (command: argument + parameter)

Hello_World

Data type - integer, boolean, list, array
Store in a variable
Access with $ prefix

Print value of variable with echo





foo="Hello World"
echo foo
echo $foo

bar=Goodbye Sky
echo $bar

foo
Hello World
bash: line 4: Sky: command not found




Why does bar=Goodbye Sky break?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Paths




File paths can be stored in variable
Two types:

Relative - start current location
Absolute - start at root

Special path: PATH

Search path of executables
Reveal command path with which

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Brace expansion




Curly braces containing a list: ‘{1..4}’
Expand sequential or comma-separated lists
Append to strings - easy file, directory generation

E.g. ‘mkdir -p sub-{1..3}’

Combine to generate permutations

E.g. ‘for i in pref-{1..3}{a..c}; do ...’

Supports nesting
Run in subshell ‘$()’ to store in variable




echo {a..d}
echo sub-{1..3}
perm=$(echo {1..3}{a..c})
nest=$(echo pref-{foo,bar{1..3},baz})
echo $perm
echo $nest

a b c d
sub-1 sub-2 sub-3
1a 1b 1c 2a 2b 2c 3a 3b 3c
pref-foo pref-bar1 pref-bar2 pref-bar3 pref-baz

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Combining variables




Access variables with ‘$’
Combine with curly braces to:

Add suff/prefix:

‘var=foo; echo ${var}bar’

Combine variables

‘var1=foo; var2=bar; echo ${var1}$var2’

Note: reuse of ‘{}’ - key-bindings are context dependent!





var1=foo; var2=bar
echo "1 ${var1}baz"
echo "2 ${var1}$var2"
echo "3 $var1$var2"
echo "4 $var1baz"

1 foobaz
2 foobar
3 foobar
4 




Why does ‘echo "4 $var1baz"’ break?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: forward removal




Often desirable to slice strings

E.g. extract “awesome” from “I_am_awesome”

Extracting subject, session, or task from file name

BIDS: sub-1_ses-A_task-memory

Combine “#” and string with variable call to slice from string beginning

“#” removes before first string match
Wildcard symbol “*” matches anything
“##” removes before final string match





bids_name=sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
echo $bids_name
echo ${bids_name#*_}
echo ${bids_name##*_}

sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
ses-A_task-memory
task-memory




What would ‘echo ${bids_name#*-}’ say?
How about ‘echo ${bids_name#sub-1}’?
How about ‘echo ${bids_name##*-}’?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: backward removal




The “%” is used to slice from the back

“%” removes after last string match
“%%” removes after first string match

An intermediate variable can be used to extract string middle




bids_name=sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
echo $bids_name
echo ${bids_name%_*}
echo ${bids_name%%_*}
int=${bids_name#*_}
echo ${int%_*}

sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
sub-1_ses-A
sub-1
ses-A

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: positional




Each character in a string has a position

0-indexed, abcd = 0123

Use “:” to specify start and end of positions




alpha="abcdefg"
echo ${alpha:0:3}
echo ${alpha:3}

abc
defg




What would ‘echo ${alpha:1:4}’ say?
What would ‘echo ${alpha:5}’ say?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: replace




Replacing substring is possible with /
Must match substring exactly
Can also be used to remove string




foo="foobbb"
echo $foo
echo "${foo/bbb/ccc}"

foobbb
fooccc




What would ‘echo "${foo/bbb/}"’ say?

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories

Anatomy of commands




Command: instruction to machine

Matches executable in PATH
Composed of arguments
Separated by spaces

Types of Arguments:

Option: modify command, specified with flag “-”
Parameter: provides information to command or option

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Foundational commands




pwd: print working directory
ls: list directory contents

ls -l: list with extra info
ls -a: list all files
ls -la: combine arguments

cd: change directories

cd foo: go down into foo
cd ..: go up one level
cd: go HOME

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Directory tree




Every file has a path
Separate steps of path with “/”
Top of path: “root”, OS essentials
Center: “~”, HOME, default
Below HOME: user files

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Make directories




mkdir: creates directory, requires parameter

mkdir foo: create directory “foo”

Many available options:

mkdir -p foo/bar: create directory “bar” within “foo” (and “foo” if it does not exist)
See more options with man mkdir

use down arrow to scroll
use “q” to exit manual


tree: see directory tree structure

Mac users: install with brew install tree

title: Computing Essentials
text:
Neuroimaging is a fascinating and exciting technique that allows researchers to “look under the hood” and study how the brain is structured, functions, and changed during development or as a result of insult. These findings have broad implications for our understanding of the human experience and help to bridge the diverse fields of biology, neuroscience, psychology, and sociology.
The modern neuroimager requires a diverse set of skills to effectively conduct their research, which include an understanding of: MRI physics, neurobiology, computer science, and advanced statistics. From the outset these can seem as a barrier to entry, especially for disciplines which may not emphasize certain technical skills.
The topics and practices here are designed to teach essential computing skills to the would-be neuroimager who has limited experience in computing, perhaps only word processing and web browsing. The topics will serve as an introductory sample to the computing skills needed to conduct collaborative research using resources at Notre Dame.
We start with understanding and writing simple blocks of code, then advance to running code on more powerful machines, and finally we will learn how to organize our compute environments and code.

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Build loops and nested loops
Skill:

Anatomy of for loop
Thinking in iterations
Nesting logic

Why:

Apply same set of commands multiple times
e.g. pipeline step for each subject

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
What is a For Loop




Purpose of computing: get computers to do the work
Computers are great at repeating work

Same command for different variables
Same workflow for different subjects

Benefits: replicability, efficiency, reduce programmer typing
For loops: special syntax to repeat series of commands
Nate’s Adage: Be clever

If repeating work, get computer to do it
Not lazy, efficient (without tendonitis)!








flowchart TB
  A[Start of list] --> B(Execute commands)
  B --> C{End of list?}
  C --> A
  C --> D[Exit]

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Anatomy of For Loops




For loops have a specific structure:

Space separated ‘for variable in list’
New line do, series of commands
Reference variable with $
New line done

Functionally:

Iterate through all items of list
Define variable from list for each iteration
Execute commands between do and done for each iteration





for var in {1..3}; do
    echo $var
done

1
2
3

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Iterating through lists




Possible to store lists

Use space between items
Account for bash returning space-separated output

Reference list in for loop syntax by variable
Best practices:

Add do to for loop definition line

“;” indicates End Of Line (EOL)

Indent to show logic levels
done on separate line, original indentation





my_sent="i am great"
num_list=$(echo {1..3})
# file_list=$(ls .)
for var in $my_sent $num_list; do
    echo $var
done

i
am
great
1
2
3

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Nesting For Loops




A child loop can exist within a parent loop
Entire child loop executed for each parent loop iteration




for num in {1..3}; do
    for alpha in {a..c}; do
        echo ${num}$alpha
    done
done

1a
1b
1c
2a
2b
2c
3a
3b
3c

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
More Best Practices




Flatter is better

Limit nesting (logic) depth to ~3 levels
Try restructuring if deeper logic is needed
Be more clever

Organize code into blocks
Have meaningful variable names

for i in {a..c} ... vs
for alpha in {a..c} ...





for num in {1..2}; do
    for alpha in {a..b}; do
        echo ${num}$alpha
    done
done
echo
for num_alpha in {1..2}{a..b}; do
    echo $num_alpha
done

1a
1b
2a
2b

1a
1b
2a
2b

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn workflow control with dependencies
Skill:

Using exit status values
Conditional statements

Why:

Avoid rebuilding existing files: increases workflow speed, decreases CPU time
Control/account for different situations (multiple tasks, data types)
Validate output to avoid downstream errors

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Exit Status




Every command returns an exit status
Held on special variable $?
0: command was successful
>0: command was unsuccessful

Each number has specific meaning





echo hi
echo $?
asdf
echo $?

hi
0
bash: line 2: asdf: command not found
127

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Use Exit Status




Special commands && and || evaluate $?
&& listens for exit status 0

if 0 (success) then process continues

|| listens for exit status >0

if >0 (fail) the process continues

Can be combined
Keep these simple!




echo hi && echo pass || echo fail
asdf && echo pass || echo fail

hi
pass
bash: line 1: asdf: command not found
fail

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Square Braces




Square braces ‘[]’ evaluate an internal statement to set exit status
Internal exit status 0: external exit status 0
Internal exit status >0: external exit status 1
White space (spaces) is very important!




[ 1 == 1 ] && echo true || echo false
[ 1 == 2 ] && echo true || echo false
[ a == a ] && echo pass $? || echo fail $?
[ a == b ] && echo pass $? || echo fail $?

true
false
pass 0
fail 1

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: if




Conditional syntax utilize square braces for workflow control

i.e. execute commands only if a condition is met

Syntax structure:

if [ assertion ]
New line then
Commands
New line fi to close conditional

Conditional work only executed if exit status = 0




if [ 1 == 1 ]; then
    echo Yay
fi
if [ 1 == 2 ]; then
    echo Nay
fi

Yay




Why is == used and not =?

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: elif




Ability to capture workflow if first conditional fails
elif (else if) assessed only when if exit status = 1
An entire new conditional is written
Read conditionals top -> bottom
Multiple elif statements allowed




foo=bat
if [ $foo == bar ]; then
    echo foobar
elif [ $foo == baz ]; then
    echo foobaz
elif [ $foo == bat ]; then
    echo foobat
fi

foobat




How many conditionals failed?
What if foo=baz?

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: else




else catches all failed conditions
Specified last
Does not evaluate an assertion




foo=foo
if [ $foo == bar ]; then
    echo foobar
elif [ $foo == baz ]; then
    echo foobaz
elif [ $foo == bat ]; then
    echo foobat
else
    echo "Unrecognized value of foo"
fi

Unrecognized value of foo

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: and




Multiple assertions can be combined with &&
As before, && only continues if exit status = 0

So, all conditionals would need to be true





foo=bar
num=1
if [ $foo == bar ] && [ $num == 1 ]; then
    echo Success
fi

Success




Would [ $num == 1 ] be assessed if foo=baz?

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: or




Assertions can also be combined with ||
As before, || only continues if exit status >0

So, only one of the assertions needs to be true

These can be combined with &&




alpha=a
num=1
if [ $alpha == b ] || [ $num == 1 ]; then
    echo Success
fi

Success




If the assertion was written [ $alpha == a ], would [ $num == 1 ] have been assessed?
Which of the assertions triggers the conditional in:




[ 1 == 2 ] && [ a == a ] || [ b == b ]

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: not




The character ! inverts logic
[ 1 != 0 ]: true ($?=0)
[ ! 1 == 0 ]: true ($?=0)
Note the white space in the second assertion
Useful to name variables to help reader through logic




[ a != b ] && echo $?
[ ! foo == bar ] && echo $?

0
0




What is printed in:




[ ! foo == bar ] && echo alpha \
    || echo beta
[ foo == bar ] || [ ! 1 == 2 ] \
    && echo delta || echo gamma

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Comparing integers




A set of special comparators operators for integers

-gt: greater than
-lt: less than
-ge: greater than or equal
-le: less than or equal
-eq: equal
-ne: not equal

Note: double parentheses are used for mathematic expressions (>, <, <=, etc)

(( 1 <= 2 ))

See more details here




[ 1 -lt 2 ] && echo 1 $?
[ ! 1 -gt 2 ] && echo 2 $?
[ 1 -le 2 ] && echo 3 $?
[ ! 1 -ge 2 ] && echo 4 $?

1 0
2 0
3 0
4 0




What is printed in:




[ ! 1 -lt 2 ] && [ 1 -eq 1 ] \
    && echo alpha || echo beta
[ 1 -gt 2 ] || [ ! 1 -ge 2 ] \
    && echo delta || echo gamma

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
File management




A set of special comparators operators for managing files

-e: something exists
-d: a directory exists
-f: a file exists
-s: a file contains data
-z: a variable is empty





[ -f foo.txt ]
[ -e foobar ]
[ -d my_dir ]
[ -z $foo ]



What is printed in:




echo "foo" > my_file.txt
[ ! -s my_file.txt ] \
    && echo alpha || echo beta

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Best practices




Keep conditionals below 3 levels of logic:

Simple, flat, short

Consider breaking up long chains into multiple statements
Inverting logic often simplifies
Name variables to help through logic

is_empty: holds boolean of whether file is empty
file_exists: holds boolean of whether file exists





# Flight control with variable
foo=""
foo_empty=$([ -z $foo ] && echo $? || echo $?)
[ $foo_empty == 0 ] && echo set_var || echo move_on

# Flight control with file
touch foo.txt
foo_exists=$([ -f foo.txt ] && echo $? || echo $?)
[ $foo_exists == 0 ] && echo move_on || echo make_foo


What would be printed in the examples above?

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn to align information across lists and build flexible for loops
Skill:

Arrays and counters
Control number of iterations

Why:

Linking information (e.g. label-anatomy)
Decrease workflow time and number of errors

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
C-style for loop




Bash supports another for loop specification:

Specify start, final, and increment values
Using numerical assessment parentheses (double)
Separated by semicolon

Only works with integers




for ((i=1; i<5; i++)); do
    echo $i
done

1
2
3
4

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Dynamic iteration control




Start and final values do not have to be hardcoded
C-style supports referencing a variable
These start and final variables could be set by another process

num_foo=$(ls foo*.txt | wc -l)





start=1
end=5
for ((i=$start; i<$end; i++)); do
    echo $i
done

1
2
3
4

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
While loops and counters




While loops can also be used to control iteration number
Syntax based on an assertion being true
Specific structure:

Space separated while [ assertion ]
New line do
Series of commands
Typically a variable is updated
New line done





cnt=1
while [ $cnt -lt 5 ]; do
    echo $cnt
    let cnt+=1
done

1
2
3
4

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Arrays




Arrays are a 0-indexed data type
Positional structure:

Defined within parentheses
Space separated

Data extracted by referencing position




arr_foo=({a..d})
arr_fruit=(apple orange banana)
echo ${arr_foo[0]}
echo ${arr_fruit[2]}

a
banana




Why was ${arr_fruit[2]} used and not ${arr_fruit[3]}?

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Arrays: position




Special syntax to reference array indices

${!arr[@]}
! queries indices
@ references all array values

Useful for iterations through array positions




arr=({a..d})
echo "Array positions are ${!arr[@]}"

for pos in ${!arr[@]}; do
    echo "Array position $pos value is ${arr[$pos]}"
done

Array positions are 0 1 2 3
Array position 0 value is a
Array position 1 value is b
Array position 2 value is c
Array position 3 value is d

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Arrays: length




Special syntax to extract array length

${#arr[@]}
# queries length

Useful for extracting positions from multiple arrays




hero=(batman superman aquaman)
color=(black red green)
echo "hero array length is ${#hero[@]}"

# Check arrays are same length
[ ${#hero[@]} == ${#color[@]} ] \
    || echo "Array length mismatch"

idx=0
while [ $idx -lt ${#hero[@]} ]; do
    echo "The hero ${hero[$idx]} wears ${color[$idx]}"
    let idx+=1
done

hero array length is 3
The hero batman wears black
The hero superman wears red
The hero aquaman wears green




Do I need to consider 0-indexing in my while assertion?
Note the extraction of array information with variable.

title: For Loops, cont’d: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Building arrays and variables




Variables and arrays can be built
Operator += allows for concatentation

In addition to increasing integer values

Command unset clears variables




unset var_foo
unset arr_foo

[ -z $var_foo ] && echo empty

for i in {1..4}; do
    var_foo+="$i"
    arr_foo+=($i)
done

[ -z $var_foo ] || echo full

echo $var_foo
echo ${var_foo[@]}

empty
full
1234
1234

text:
Why learn to use a cluster


Modern MRI: large data initiatives

Human Connectome Project (HCP)
Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD)
Data repositories (OpenNeuro, NIMH, FITBIR)

Complicated analytic pipelines

title: Cluster Computing: what is it, login, move data
text:
Description of cluster



The Center for Research Computing (CRC) provides cluster computing resources

Network of compute nodes (~8K CPUs) and RAM

Their Wiki contains valuable resources for accessing, using cluster
Main components

Login point: manage data, submit requests
Scheduler: index resources, manage request queue
Cluster: CPUs and RAM
Storage: file system








flowchart TB
  A[Work Machine] -- Internet --> B[Login Node]
  B -- Scheduler --> C[Cluster]
  B --> D[File Structure]
  C --> D








Resist running processes on login node! They will be killed.

title: Cluster Computing: what is it, login, move data
text:
Moving data: scp


scp: Copy files over an SSH connection

Copy entire file or directory

Anatomy of command:

scp [OPTS] source destination
Separate computer from path with ‘:’

Can be used to both push and pull data:

scp file.txt user@crcfe01.crc.nd.edu:~

Send file.txt from local to CRC home

scp -r user@crcfe01.crc.nd.edu:~/project ~/Desktop

Pull ~/project directory from CRC to the local desktop


See here for more details

title: Cluster Computing: what is it, login, move data
text:
Moving data: rsync


Do not often desire to send entire directory

e.g. files exist at src and dst, new files made at src

rsync: Index both src and dst

Move only difference

Anatomy of command:

rsync [OPTS] source destination

Similar to scp, can both push and pull data

rsync -rauv ~/project user@crcfe01.crc.nd.edu:~
Compares local project to remote, sends any difference

See here for more details

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn to build and manage environments
Skill:

Activate conda
Build and manage environments
Save and remove environments

Why:

Manage software version dependencies
Work within a consistent environment

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Need for conda


Research involves specific software

As software develops, new versions function differently
Software suites often call on other suites
Software version can have specific hardware requirements
Together, a chance for dependency hell

Projects take years:

Need to hold versions constant for on-going projects
Need to use newer versions for new projects

Replication dependent on specific software versions
Conda is a package and environment manager

Build environments with specific software versions

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Conda on the CRC



Conda is provided as a module on the CRC

See here for their documentation
Find module via module avail | grep conda

Activate conda via:

module load conda
conda init
source ~/.bashrc

Why use source instead of ./?

module unload conda

Verify via conda info

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Named environments



Environments can be named

Purposes (e.g. python3.8, r4.1)
Projects (e.g. rest_fmri, proj_name)

Use conda by envoking command conda and supply arguments
conda create -n test_name: build named environment test_name

Note the build location in ~/.conda

conda env list: see available environments
conda activate test_name: activate test_name enironment
conda deactivate: exits environment

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Prefix (path) environments



All named envs have paths
Possible to make only prefixed (path) envs

Save env to specific location
Make env available to other users (e.g. RAs)

conda create -p ~/test_path
Note:

the build location
Absence of a name

Activate by path
Tip: add env_prompt: '({name})' to .condarc to only see the name of env (and not full path)

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Installing packages



conda list: show packages installed in current env
conda install: install specific package name

Default is to search for package at conda-forge

conda install -c conda-forge python=3.10: install python version 3.10 from conda-forge repository into current env
Note: strength of conda - also installs dependencies!

And manages versions if conflicts arise
Only when installed through conda, not other package managers (e.g. pip)

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Multiple environments



Environments do not conflict with each other
Separate environments allow for separate software versions
Applicable to Python, R, Java, C, C++, and others
Useful for differing projects!
Recommendation: one environment per project

Allows to lock in versions
Enables newer versions for newer projects

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Exporting environments



Saving environment:

Backup
Share with collaborators
Add to code repository

conda env export > env_name.yml: save environment as YAML file

Preferred method

conda list --explicit > env_name.txt: save environment sources as text file

Not as robust

Environments can be built from files using the -f option (see here)

title: Conda: environments and software
text:
Deleting environments



Clean unused environments

Can always rebuild from backup file
(Assuming versions work on hardware or OS version)

Removal is similar to creation

conda env remove -n test_name: remove named env test_name
conda env remove -p ~/test_path: remove previx env test_path

Foundational skillset for research and industry

title: Git and GitHub: tracking changes
text:
Git



Git is software designed to track changes

“Who did what and when”
Resolved version control problems on collaborative projects

Monitors requested directories and files

Creates a log of what changed and how

Control Git with a series of simple commands
Native in Linux distributions

Need to install in Windows, Mac






https://git-scm.com

title: Git and GitHub: tracking changes
text:
GitHub



GitHub is a centralized platform
Allows developers to create, store, manage, share their code
Great for research:

Redundancy
Transparency
Collaboration
Internal reliability
External replicability

Create an account





https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GitHub

title: Git and GitHub: tracking changes
text:
Setup: CRC



Git provided with default login shell
Need to:

Configure git for your user
Connect git to your GitHub account

title: Git and GitHub: tracking changes
text:
Setup: config files



Create config file: ~/.gitconfig
Copy provided code to ~/.gitconfig

Whitespace (tabs) included
Provide your name (will be added to git logs)
Provide email address (will be added to git logs)

Many config options available, we will keep it simple here



[credential]
    helper = store
[user]
    name = <your name>
    email = <your github email>

You’re done!
